MINUTES
  ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  MARCH 26, 2025

  CHAIR STEGURA called the meeting of the Environmental Advisory Committee Meeting of the
  City of Rolling Hills Estates at 7:00 p.m.

  2.  ROLL CALL

  COMMITTEE MEMBERS PRESENT:  Stegura, Bain, Chuang, McBurney, Rapoport, Uppal,

  COMMITTEE MEMBERS ABSENT:  Rein, Repp-Loadsman, Schmidt

  STAFF MEMBERS PRESENT:  Jeannie Naughton, Community Development Director
  Whitney Berry, Senior Planner
  Carol Corea, Administrative Analyst

  3.  APPROVAL OF MINUTES

  A.  APPROVAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING MINUTES,
  MARCH 3, 2024.

  COMMISSIONER BAIN made a motion, seconded by COMMITTEE MEMBER RAPOPORT to,

  APPROVE THE CORRECTED ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEEETING
  MINUTES OF MARCH 6, 2024.

  There being no objection, CHAIR STEGURA so ordered.

  4.  AUDIENCE ITEMS/ORAL COMMUNICATION ON ITEMS NOT ON THE AGENDA

  NONE

  5.  DISCUSSION ITEMS

  A.  PLASTIC POLLUTION PREVENTION

  Senior Planner Berry provided a presentation with an overview of the State's plastic pollution
  prevention efforts, including SB 54. She stated that other bills have recently been passed and the
  City responded by updating its ordinance on single-use food ware accessories. She stated that
  this item came before the committee due to a letter from the PVP California League of Women
  Voters received by the City Council. There were several subsequent meetings since the letter was
  received in 2023. At the last EAC meeting, the committee directed staff to focus on outreach to
  stakeholders to align efforts and to investigate educational programs to move away from
  polystyrene food containers and opt for other sustainable containers.

  CHAIR STEGURA asked if the school district is using recyclable/compostable food containers in
  its cafeterias. COMMITTEE MEMBER UPPAL stated that she believes so but will confirm if this is
  the case.

ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
  1
MEETING, MARCH 26, 2025
   Senior Planner Berry stated that the objective of SB54 was to shift the responsibility of the plastic
  pollution problem to the manufacturers by requiring them to demonstrate the type of material they
  are using to be recyclable/compostable. She stated that Governor Newson put a pause on this bill.
  Senior Planner Berry stated that staff will continue to track this and hope to bring the committee
  updates in the future.

  Senior Planner Berry summarized staff’s outreach efforts, including discussion this with PVP
  Chamber of Commerce, PVP League of Women Voters, and the Surfrider Foundation.

  Senior Planner Berry stated that she had a conversation with Rethink Disposables and explained
  that there is a pass-through fund, possibly grant money, that goes through the city to be distributed
  for services and stated that Rethink Disposables can purchase bulk quantities of disposables.
  These are distributed to the businesses who have applied through the city for these services.

  Senior Planner Berry stated that the South Bay Cities Council of Governments (SBCCOG)
  managed a Green Business Network Program, which was being funded by a state grant. She
  stated that the SBCCOG program is on hold; however, there is an effort to coordinate and expand
  the Los Angeles County Green Business program, which is similar to ReThink Disposables’
  program.

  Senior Planner Berry shared Mill Valley's implementation of a plastic ban ordinance. She noted
  that operating in a context where the county had a ban made enforcement more straightforward.
  She further noted that enforcement was not the primary means of implementation, and rather was
  more incentive based.

  Senior Planner Berry stated that staff recommend that the EAC discuss this item and if they wish
  to direct staff to work with the SBCCOG to advocate for the Green Business Program to be
  expanded to include RHE and other cities.

  CHAIR STEGURA stated that she was under the impression that the polystyrene ban was in effect
  beginning on January 1, 2025; however, there is no way to enforce it. The City previously
  implemented Heal the Bay’s restaurant certification program, that included inspections for the
  program’s requirements as part of the City’s stormwater permit, but Heal the Bay is no longer
  administering the program.

  Director Naughton mentioned that the City still conducts restaurant inspections, mainly for
  stormwater runoff, but they also check for sustainability items. She suggested creating a city-
  branded program similar to Heal the Bay, including stickers and a basic program structure.

  Senior Planner Berry proposed creating a small program for restaurants in Rolling Hills Estates,
  which has the bulk of restaurants in the area. She suggested educating local restaurants about SB
  54 compliance and providing information on vendors for compliant materials.

  COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN asked if a small program could be created to see what restaurants
  are using polystyrene. Director Naughton stated that currently, no restaurants in the city use
  polystyrene.

  In response to a question by COMMITTEE MEMBER RAPAPORT, Senior Planner Berry
  mentioned that at the last meeting she shared a table comparing different cities in the South Bay
  that have implemented similar programs, including their enforcement methods. She noted that the
  previous direction from the EAC was to put a hold on creating an ordinance due to its complexity

ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
  2
MEETING, MARCH 26, 2025
   and potential enforcement difficulties and instead focus on aligning with SB 54. Senior Planner
  Berry agreed to gather more information about how the LA County program works in this regard.
  COMMITTEE MEMBER UPPAL asked about any rules/regulations on composting. Director
  Naughton stated that there are new requirements for organic food waste for non-residential
  accounts.

  COMMITTEE MEMBER MCBURNEY noted that some businesses, like Chipotle, had previously
  implemented separate bins for composting but have changed their practices. He suggested
  interfacing with PV school gardens to promote education about composting and the use of
  compostable utensils.

  CHAIR STEGURA stated that Waste Management has been a good partner to educate the
  community on putting food scraps out with yard waste.

  COMMITTEE MEMBER MCBURNEY mentioned that some of the surrounding cities have worked
  with their waste haulers to bring back the composted material for residents to use in their gardens.
  Director Naughton suggested reaching out to Waste Management to do this for the City’s Earth
  Day event.

  COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN asked if the committee would endorse staff to organize a program
  to identify the restaurants, inventory current practices, bring a recommendation of standard of
  practices, get approval from the PVP Chamber of Commerce, and implement a program.

  CHAIR STEGURA stated that she believes that the Chamber would not be opposed to an
  education program for businesses but expressed concern with asking businesses to be 100%
  compostable by 2032 when regulation has been suspended.

  COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN made a motion, seconded by COMMITTEE MEMBER RAPAPORT
  to,

  DIRECT STAFF TO COORDINATE WITH THE PVP CHAMBER OF COMMERCE PUT
  TOGETHER A PROGRAM ALONG WITH THE EXISTING RESTAURANT STORMWATER
  INSPECTIONS AND ADD A QUESTION REGARDING THE TYPES OF CONTAINERS
  AND UTENSILS USED FOR TAKEOUT. WITH THAT DATA, WORK WITH THE CHAMBER
  TO EDUCATE RESTAURANTS PROVIDING INFORMATION ON WHERE THE LAW IS
  GOING AND TO CREATE A VISIBLE RECOGNITION FOR EARLY ADOPTERS.

  There being no objection, CHAIR STEGURA so ordered.

  B.  SUSTAINABILITY ELEMENT IMPLEMENTATION

  Director Naughton provided an overview and purpose of the Sustainability Element and explained
  that it is an optional element, for which the City received a grant to prepare and was adopted with
  the updated General Plan in 2022.

  Director Naughton stated that Title 24 is the energy code in California Building Code and the last
  update was in 2022 and this year is a code cycle update. Clean Power Alliance (CPA) has two
  grant programs that the City is already involved in.

  Director Naughton stated that the City established a bonus level development program in the
  commercial district. She stated that the first project was approved in December which incorporated
  community amenities, including public parking and improved connectivity between the Peninsula
  Center and the Promenade as well as 15% moderate-income units as a part of the project. She

ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
  3
MEETING, MARCH 26, 2025
   stated that this project will be 90 units, and 9 units will be moderate income. The discussion turned
  to the possibility of adopting an incentive-based reach program for sustainable development.

  Director Naughton suggested pursuing an incentive-based reach code program that could serve
  as an option for sustainable development as a qualifier for community amenities in the commercial
  district.

  Director Naughton stated that CPA is extending technical support through 2025 for reach code
  pathways. The CPA provides technical support and a packaged code but noted that city staff would
  still be responsible for community outreach and stakeholder engagement.

  Director Naughton explained that if this program is approved, amendments would need to be
  adopted to the LA County Code and the Green Building Standard Code. She further explained the
  need to update reach codes every three years, which would require hiring someone to review and
  amend the city’s code.

  In response to a question by COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN, Director Naughton stated that the
  developer would be able to build more residential units and further explained bonus level
  development.

  Director Naughton stated that the Power Ready Program proposes to provide solar and battery
  backup for community critical facilities at no upfront cost. She stated that the program has
  expanded beyond city-owned facilities to include community partner-owned critical facilities that
  might serve as cooling centers or emergency gathering places.

  Director Naughton invited the committee to suggest potential community critical facilities that could
  benefit from this program. She offered to have a CPA representative provide a detailed
  presentation to answer any questions the committee might have.

  In response to a question by COMMITTEE MEMBER UPPAL, Director Naughton stated that for
  the Power Ready program, the CPA would do a feasibility analysis, and if feasible will install, and
  provide the electric generator that could support critical electric loads as battery backup.

  COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN inquired about eligibility requirements. Director Naughton stated
  that they need to act as a cooling center or emergency evacuation center or something similar.

  COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN made a motion, seconded by COMMITTEE MEMBER MCBURNEY
  to,

  DIRECT STAFF TO BRING EXPERTISE ON THE REACH CODE AND POWER READY
  PROGRAM TO THE NEXT EAC MEETING.

  There being no objection, CHAIR STEGURA so ordered.

  COMMITTEE MEMBER RAPAPORT suggested adding a polystyrene ban to the reach code.
  Director Naughton stated that the reach codes are specific to building construction and this section
  of code does not regulate the operation of businesses.

  COMMITTEE MEMBER MCBURNEY stated that he supports the idea of exploring the polystyrene
  ban. He would also like to know where the interruption is happening with food waste pathway. If it
  is room for dumpsters, he questioned if this could be added. Director Naughton stated that this
  could be required for new developments.

ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE

MEETING, MARCH 26, 2025
   6.  DIRECTOR ITEMS

  Director Naughton provided an update on e-bikes, which was prepared by Jessica Slawson,
  Assistant to the City Manager.

  7.  COMMITTEE ITEMS/FUTURE AGENDA ITEMS

  CHAIR STEGURA provided a brief overview on the role of the EAC and explained that it is an
  advisory committee to the City Council.

  8.  ADJOURNMENT

  CHAIR STEGURA adjourned the meeting at 8:26 p.m.
